summary: Describes the liaison and working relationship between the IETF and Cable Television Laboratories (CableLabs), covering how the two organizations collaborate on standards work. It is an informational administrative memo.

eli5.summary: A note about how two groups, one for the internet and one for cable TV, agree to work together.

subtitle: How IETF and cable television standards bodies collaborate.

tldr.problem: Cable Television Laboratories (CableLabs) and the IETF develop overlapping standards for technologies used in cable networks. Without formal coordination, the organizations risk duplicating work or creating incompatible specifications.
tldr.mechanism: This document establishes a liaison relationship with designated managers, procedures for document sharing, and formal communication channels (liaison statements) between the two organizations.
tldr.outcome: The two bodies now have a framework for coordinating work, exchanging requirements, and ensuring interoperability with existing Internet systems.

facts.label: Public availability
facts.value: All IETF liaison statements published as public documents

today: RFC 4965 remains the active liaison agreement between IETF and CableLabs. The document is Informational and has not been obsoleted or updated. Both organizations continue to operate under this framework, with liaison managers facilitating coordination on standards that affect cable networks and the Internet.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Cable Television Laboratories, Inc. (CableLabs) is a research and development consortium of cable operators, manufacturers, and vendors. It develops standards for cable technologies like DOCSIS (Data Over Cable Service Interface Specification), PacketCable, and OpenCable. The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) develops Internet standards through open working groups and a consensus-based process.

Both organizations touch related technologies. CableLabs uses IETF standards like DHCP, SIP, and IP routing in its cable systems. The IETF needs to understand cable network requirements to ensure its standards work well with cable deployments. This document formalizes their collaboration, establishing principles for how they will work together, share specifications, and communicate.
sections.eli5: CableLabs makes rules for cable TV networks. The IETF makes rules for the Internet. Both use similar technologies, so they need to work together.

sections.title: Basis of Collaboration
sections.content:
The two organizations agree that CableLabs will preferentially use IETF standards unchanged whenever feasible, rather than creating proprietary alternatives. However, CableLabs recognizes that it may need to request modifications or extensions to IETF standards to meet cable-specific requirements.

When CableLabs needs changes to an IETF specification, it can raise issues directly with the relevant IETF working groups. If no suitable working group exists or informal working group discussion is insufficient, the issue goes through liaison managers—named representatives who can formally communicate between the organizations.

The IETF may also ask CableLabs questions about its requirements or offer guidance on effective use of IETF standards. Both organizations operate by their own rules, governance, and intellectual property policies, but they commit to avoiding duplication of work and supporting each other's specifications.
sections.eli5: CableLabs will try to use the IETF's rules instead of making its own. When they need changes, they ask nicely. The two groups have people whose job is to talk to each other.

sections.title: Document Sharing and Public Availability
sections.content:
All IETF documents are publicly available from the IETF Web site. CableLabs publishes certain documents in its public repository with ISSUED status, making them available at http://www.cablelabs.com/specifications/.

For either organization to reference the other's work (normatively or informatively), the document must be in an approved, published, publicly available state. CableLabs individuals can contribute to IETF by submitting documents as IETF Contributions, following IETF intellectual property procedures without requiring non-disclosure agreements.

The two organizations agree to maintain and regularly update a list of dependencies between their respective specifications and work in progress, ensuring each understands what the other is doing.
sections.eli5: Both groups share their finished rules publicly. When one wants to refer to the other's work, the document must be published and freely available.

sections.title: Liaison Managers and Formal Communication
sections.content:
Each organization appoints a liaison manager as a primary contact. The CableLabs liaison manager to IETF works with CableLabs projects and IETF working groups to facilitate interaction. The IETF appoints a liaison manager to CableLabs, appointed by the Internet Architecture Board (IAB), to serve as an initial contact for administrative aspects of collaboration that cannot be handled informally.

When formal communication is needed, it proceeds through liaison statements, following procedures defined in RFC 4053. All IETF liaison statements are published as public documents. The liaison managers help route communications to the appropriate working groups, areas, or senior leadership in each organization.

Participation in IETF is open to any individual, including those who work for CableLabs member companies or vendors. Such individuals can freely contribute to IETF mailing lists, submit drafts, attend meetings, and help the IETF understand cable requirements.
sections.eli5: Each group picks a person to be the official talker to the other group. When they need to say something important, they write it down and send it officially, and it is published so everyone can see it.

sections.title: Scope and Common Work Areas
sections.content:
The document lists IETF working groups of particular interest to CableLabs, including groups focused on DHCP, Kerberos, SIP, IPv6, IP Security, DNS, TLS, and network management. CableLabs and IETF members can participate in these groups to align cable and Internet technologies.

The two organizations explicitly do not co-develop documents. Each maintains its own development and approval processes, governed by its own rules. The collaboration is a coordination mechanism, not a merger of processes.

CableLabs mailing lists are not open to the general public, so work of mutual interest is discussed on IETF mailing lists where anyone can participate. This maintains IETF openness while accommodating CableLabs' membership model.
sections.eli5: They share interest in many topics like IP routing and security. They do not create documents together, but they follow each other's work and stay in touch.
